In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
clogging evolution is strongly influenced by the type and distribution of the vegetation in the basin.
the major clogging is located at the bottom of the basin, that it is mainly due to the vegetation and that its spatial distribution is heterogeneous with some preferential zones.

the clogging evolution in time and space of the studied infiltration basin can be described by a combination of the following three main mechanisms: (i) sedimentation of fine particles in the basin bottom, (ii) vegetation growth and (iii) sedimentation of particles at the basin sides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(i) the global scale study revealed that clogging was mainly located on the sides and on the bottom and (ii) the local scale study showed that clogging was spatially heterogeneous and that the presence of vegetation was beneficial for the hydraulic conductivity of the soil.
the global scale monitoring is a very good tool to monitor clogging evolution in time and to identify the part due to the bottom, due to the sides or both.
clogging evolution is a complex issue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
clogging evolution is not uniform in time and space and it is not the same on different types of vegetation.
clogging is not homogeneous in the infiltration systems studied, and that it evolves in space and time.
clogging of storm-water infiltration systems is a dynamic process that is strongly related to vegetation.
